title: How to Balance Airflow Between Rooms
h1: How Do You Balance Airflow Between Rooms in Your Home?
description: Balancing airflow between rooms starts with clean filters, open vents and duct damper adjustments. Learn what you can do yourself and when to call a pro.
quick_answer: Start by changing the filter and making sure every supply and return vent is open and clear. Then use the dampers on your branch ducts, if you have them, to send less air to rooms that are too cold and more to rooms that are too warm. Make small changes and wait a day between them. If that doesn't work, the ducts may need repair, sealing or zoning.
body:
Most homes have at least one room that never feels quite right. Balancing the airflow means adjusting how much air goes to each room so the house feels more even. Some of it you can do yourself. Some of it needs a technician with the right tools.

Why is airflow uneven in the first place?

Air takes the easiest path. Rooms close to the furnace or air handler with short duct runs tend to get plenty of air, while rooms at the end of long runs get less. Other common causes include:

  • Leaky or disconnected ducts in the attic
  • Crushed or kinked flex duct
  • Ducts that are too small for the room they serve
  • Not enough return air, especially in bedrooms with closed doors
  • Rooms with big west-facing windows or above the garage
  • Second floors, where heat naturally collects

What can I do before adjusting anything?

Start with the basics. They fix more problems than you'd think:

  1. Replace the air filter.
  2. Open every supply register and move furniture, rugs and curtains away from vents.
  3. Check that return grilles aren't blocked and that their filters, if any, are clean.
  4. Look in the attic, if you can do it safely, for ducts that are disconnected, crushed or lying loose.
  5. Use window coverings on sunny sides of the house during the hottest part of the day.

How do I use balancing dampers?

Many duct systems have manual dampers on the branch ducts, usually near where they connect to the main trunk or supply plenum. They look like a small lever or wing nut on the side of the duct. When the lever lines up with the duct, the damper is open. When it's across the duct, it's closed.

Here's a simple process:

  1. Set the thermostat to a normal temperature and let the system run.
  2. Note which rooms run warm or cool. A cheap thermometer in each room helps.
  3. Partly close the dampers to rooms that get too much air. Don't close them all the way.
  4. Wait a day and check temperatures again.
  5. Repeat with small adjustments until the house is more even.

In a two-story home, you may want different settings for summer and winter. In summer, send more air upstairs. In winter, send a bit more downstairs, since warm air rises on its own. Mark the damper positions with a marker so you can switch back easily.

Should I close vents in rooms I don't use?

Closing one or two registers is usually fine. Closing many of them is a bad idea. It raises pressure in the ducts, which can push more air out through leaks, reduce airflow across the coil and make the system work harder. In some cases, it can lead to a frozen AC coil or an overheating furnace.

When do I need a professional?

If simple adjustments don't help, the problem is usually in the duct system itself. A technician can measure airflow at each register, check static pressure and find leaks or undersized ducts. Common fixes include:

  • Sealing and repairing leaky or disconnected ducts
  • Replacing crushed flex duct and rerouting long runs
  • Adding dampers where there are none
  • Adding return air paths, such as transfer grilles or jumper ducts, for bedrooms
  • Installing a zoning system with motorized dampers and separate thermostats
  • Adding a ductless mini-split for a room the main system can't reach

Our HVAC technicians handle airflow testing, zoning and system adjustments, and our air duct team takes care of duct sealing and repair.

How do I know the balance is right?

When rooms on the same floor stay within a couple of degrees of each other and the system isn't running nonstop, you're in good shape. Some difference between floors is normal, especially in two-story homes during inland heat.

Keep in mind that balancing isn't a one-time job. Furniture moves, rooms change use and seasons shift, so it is worth checking temperatures again at the start of summer and winter. A few small adjustments each season usually keep the house feeling even.
faqs: Where are the dampers on my ducts?

Look on the round branch ducts near where they leave the main trunk or supply box, usually in the attic, garage or above a hall closet. You'll see a small lever or wing nut on the outside of the duct.
Can closing vents damage my HVAC system?
Closing a lot of vents can. It raises pressure in the ducts, reduces airflow across the coil and can cause a frozen AC coil or an overheating furnace. Close only a few, partially.
Why is my upstairs always hotter?
Heat rises, the roof heats the upstairs rooms, and those rooms are often at the end of long duct runs. Adjusting dampers, sealing ducts, adding returns or zoning can help.
Is zoning worth it for a two-story house?
Zoning often helps two-story homes because each floor gets its own thermostat and the system sends air where it's needed. It works best when the ductwork is in good shape.
